Radius and direction

Four points.
Three visits.

The ellipse offers four points at the same radius. Three return to the same place on the orbital drawing. The fourth passes in another direction.

Thirty, sixty, then one hundred twenty folds: three selected meetings creep toward the same radial shoulder. Each is a negative ordinary triple. At its exact location, three visits meet and a fourth is excluded.

One radius is only half the test

A point in the orbital drawing has both a radius and a direction. The ellipse's four candidates share the first. They usually do not share the second. At these selected phases, three agree on both; the fourth cannot.

The radius equation is a quartic. Three known roots leave just one candidate. Its possible time direction would have to satisfy one more circle identity. Rational bounds prove it misses that identity in all three examples.

Closer to the shoulder

No three-or-more-visit meeting is possible through 0.894940827171…π, at any positive fold count. These examples get closer as their folds grow. A separate analytic argument constructs meetings arbitrarily close from above, with phase excess proportional to 1/d².

The finite examples certify selected batches, with thirty, sixty, or one hundred twenty rotated points each. They do not count every event at those fold counts, identify the first meeting, or supply a numerical cutoff for the analytic theorem. The drawings and printed phase locations are rounded illustrations.

Ordinary triples reach the same limit

A further analytic calculation proves that ordinary negative triples approach the shoulder too. For sufficiently large folds, all three selected pairs stay transverse, and a fourth branch cannot join at two consecutive fold counts. At least one of each pair therefore has an ordinary triple. There is no specified starting fold count.

The meeting also gets flatter: its closest pair of tangent directions approaches parallel as 1/d³. Follow the tangent expansion and the fourth direction ↗.
